title: Delhi Traffic Police Announce Vehicle Entry Curbs Under Revised GRAP From November 1
excerpt: Only BS-VI, CNG, electric and exempt vehicles may enter the capital from November 1, with more than 10 lakh NCR vehicles below the standard.
body:
• From November 1, only BS-VI, CNG, electric and exempt-category vehicles may enter Delhi under the revised GRAP rules announced by Delhi Traffic Police on October 30.
  • Vehicles without a valid Pollution Under Control Certificate (PUCC) also face restriction, and non-compliant interstate buses are covered.
  • The bar on non-BS-VI vehicles registered outside Delhi runs until January 31, 2027; transport department estimates count more than 10 lakh such vehicles across Delhi-NCR.
  • Drivers can check eligibility via the traffic police helplines 011-25844444 and 1095 before travelling.

Delhi Traffic Police announced fresh vehicle entry restrictions under the revised Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) on Thursday, effective November 1, urging motorists to check their vehicle's eligibility before travelling to the capital. Under the advisory, reported by IANS and carried by NDTV, only BS-VI-compliant vehicles, CNG vehicles, electric vehicles and exempted categories will be allowed entry, subject to the applicable rules.

Who is barred, who is exempt

The restrictions apply to vehicles that do not meet BS-VI emission standards and to those without a valid Pollution Under Control Certificate. Non-compliant interstate buses face restrictions, and only electric, CNG and BS-VI diesel buses may operate into the region. Trucks not destined for Delhi must use the peripheral expressways instead of entering the city, and restrictions also apply to tractors and jugaad vehicles and to certain vehicles registered outside Delhi, according to the traffic police advisory reported by IANS. The separate bar on non-BS-VI vehicles registered outside Delhi runs from November 1 until January 31, 2027. CNG and electric vehicles are exempt, as are ambulances, fire tenders and specified essential services; vehicles registered inside Delhi are not covered by that particular provision, though age and other pollution rules still apply to them.

The scale: more than 10 lakh vehicles

Transport department estimates cited in the reporting put more than 10 lakh vehicles across Noida, Greater Noida, Gurugram, Faridabad and Ghaziabad below BS-VI standards. Noida and Greater Noida together account for more than four lakh, Ghaziabad for around four lakh, and Gurugram and Faridabad for nearly two lakh — about 70 percent of them BS-III or BS-IV, including roughly 50,000 commercial vehicles in the two Haryana districts, according to IANS reporting on the November 1 bar. Enforcement will lean on AI-powered automatic number plate recognition cameras at entry points, alongside physical checks. Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa has reviewed implementation with traffic police and NCR district officials, and the traffic police say more than 10,000 challans a day are already being issued for traffic and pollution violations, The CSR Journal reported.

Enforcement has already started

The announcement follows a special drive on October 27 in which Northern Range traffic police registered three FIRs against commercial vehicle operators allegedly using fake No Entry Permissions at Delhi's border areas, under Sections 318(2) and 340(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, on the directions of DCP (Traffic) Dr Sachin Kumar Singhal. The Commission for Air Quality Management had invoked Stage I of GRAP on October 21 after Delhi's air quality slipped into the poor category; the city's overall AQI was recently recorded at 168, with PM2.5 and PM10 the primary pollutants.

What commuters should do now

Anyone driving into Delhi from the NCR in a petrol or diesel vehicle should confirm two things before November 1: that the vehicle meets BS-VI norms, and that its PUCC is valid. If either fails, the vehicle should not attempt entry — display boards are planned at border checkpoints, and the traffic police helplines, 011-25844444 and 1095, are open for eligibility questions. For families with relatives in the capital — and for diaspora readers with homes and vehicles in the NCR — the January 31 end date matters: this is a three-month winter regime, not a one-week emergency measure, and GRAP stages can still add further curbs on top if air quality worsens.
